storyline: No one lives long enough to watch a star grow up, so astronomers do what a visitor to a forest might: find trees of every age and put them in order. This journey does the same with the sky. It starts in a cloud of gas and dust where gravity is making stars right now, then moves to a newborn cluster that is blowing its birth cloud away. Next comes a family that has lived in the open for millions or billions of years and lost its heaviest members. From there it follows one star into old age, swollen into a giant, and then to a star on the brink, down to its last fuels or already shedding its skin. It ends, where the sky allows, with what a star leaves behind: a glowing shell, the wreck of a supernova, or the cooling ember of a white dwarf. Each stop is the stage that follows the one before, and the thread that ties them is weight, because the heavier a star, the faster it lives and the more violently it dies.

title.A1-cradle-to-grave: How the Stars of {region} Grow Old
Where Are {region}'s Stars in Their Lives?
question.A1-cradle-to-grave: Where do stars come from, and how do they end?
What happens to a star between its birth and its death?
How can one night's sky show the whole life of a star?
hook.A1-cradle-to-grave: No one lives long enough to watch a star grow up, yet the sky shows every age at once.
A star's life is far too long to watch, so we read it from many stars of different ages.
The gas a dying star gives back becomes the next stars, and you can follow the cycle.
story.A1-cradle-to-grave: Astronomers learn a star's life the way you might learn a forest's, by finding trees of every age and putting them in order. Tonight you do the same around {region}, from {hook} to {name}.

Every star you can see is at some point in one life story: born in a cold cloud, raised in a family, swollen in old age and finally returned to space. Tonight each stop is a different moment of that life, in the order a star lives it.
Stars are not eternal, and their weight decides how fast they live and how they die. Starting at {hook}, you follow that life forward to its end, one stage at a time.
payoff.A1-cradle-to-grave: The sky holds every stage of a star's life at once, because stars of every age are shining side by side. They condense from cold clouds, live on the fuel in their cores for millions or billions of years, and grow old from the top down, the heaviest first. Weight sets the pace, and it decides how violent the ending will be. In the end each gives its gas back to space, richer in elements than it was at birth, and from clouds of that recycled gas the Sun, the Earth and everything on it were made.

From {hook} to {name} you have followed a single life by reading many. Gravity gathers a cloud into stars, the newborns clear their cradle and live as a family, and each member ages at a pace set by its weight. Old age swells a star into a giant, and the end returns its matter to space, enriched with elements the star made. Nothing is wasted, because that matter becomes the next nursery, and long ago some of it became the Sun, the Earth and us.

No single star lives quickly enough to watch, but the sky holds every stage at once. It shows collapsing clouds and newborn families, older families that have lost their heaviest members, and giants swelling toward their last fuels. The heavier a star, the faster it runs through that sequence and the more violently it ends. What it finally gives back seeds the next generation of stars, and our own Sun and planet were built from such gifts.
payoff.A1-cradle-to-grave.end6: The sky holds every stage of a star's life at once, and tonight you read them in order, ending at {name}, what a star leaves behind. Clouds collapse into stars, families age from the top down, and old age swells each star until its fuel is gone. Then a star like the Sun lets its layers drift off around a cooling core, while a heavyweight collapses and explodes. Either way its gas returns to space richer than it began, and from such recycled gas the Sun, the Earth and we ourselves were made.

From {hook} to {name} you have followed one life by reading many, all the way to its end, with weight setting how fast each star lived. The end hands a star's matter back to the clouds, enriched with carbon and other elements it forged, and {name} is one such gift on its way back. In time it will be gathered into a new nursery, the same road that the material of the Sun and the Earth once took.
payoff.A1-cradle-to-grave.end5: The sky holds every stage of a star's life at once, and tonight you read them in order, as far as {name}, a star on the brink. Clouds collapse into stars, families age from the top down, and old age swells each star until only its last fuels are left. After that, weight decides the rest: a star of modest mass lets its outer layers go around a cooling core, while a heavyweight collapses and explodes. Either way its gas returns to space richer than it began, and from such gas the Sun, the Earth and we ourselves were made.

From {hook} to {name} you have followed one life by reading many, right to the edge of its end, with weight setting how fast each star got there. {name} is nearly out of fuel, and when it finishes, its matter will go back to the clouds, enriched with elements it forged. That is the same road the material of the Sun and the Earth once took.
story.A1-cradle-to-grave.end6: Tonight's stars are one life told by many, each caught a stage later than the one before. The night begins at {hook} and ends at {name}, with what a star leaves behind once its life is over.

Every star you will see tonight is at a different moment of the same life, and the stops run in the order a star lives them, right through to its death. Weight is the thread: the heavier a star, the faster it travels that road and the more violently it ends.
story.A1-cradle-to-grave.end5: Tonight's stars are one life told by many, each caught a stage later than the one before. The night begins at {hook} and ends at {name}, a star on the brink of its own ending.

Every star you will see tonight is at a different moment of the same life, and the stops run in the order a star lives them, as far as a star close to its end. Weight is the thread: the heavier a star, the faster it travels that road.

DN-Coalsack.beat: Before birth: a cold dark cloud
DN-Coalsack.question: Could the Coalsack one day become a nursery like those of Carina?
DN-Coalsack.why: Every star's life starts in cold, dark gas, and the Coalsack is that raw material in its purest form, so close that it shows as a shadow on the Milky Way.
DN-Coalsack.answer: It may one day, but not yet: studies of its gas suggest it has made no stars at all. To begin, parts of it must grow dense enough for gravity to beat the pressure of the gas. A push from outside, such as the light of hot stars or the shock of a dying one, often supplies the squeeze, which is how one generation of stars sets off the next.
DN-Coalsack.story: A cloud like this is held up against its own weight by the restless churning of its gas and by magnetic fields threaded through it, and only where those give way can a clump begin to fall inward. Radio telescopes tuned to molecules such as carbon monoxide weigh the gas and search it for the dense knots where that collapse starts, and in the Coalsack they find almost none.

DN-Pipe.beat: Before birth: a cold dark cloud
DN-Pipe.question: Why has this huge dark cloud made so few stars?
DN-Pipe.why: Before there is a nursery there is a cloud, and the Pipe is one of the nearest, a silhouette of cold gas and dust laid across the brightest part of the Milky Way.
DN-Pipe.answer: Over most of the Pipe gravity has not yet won. A cloud makes stars only where a clump grows dense enough for its own weight to overcome the pressure of the gas inside it. In the Pipe that has happened in earnest in one place, Barnard 59, at the western end of the stem, and the rest is raw material, waiting, as the glowing nurseries of Sagittarius once were.
DN-Pipe.story: Astronomers mapped the Pipe by measuring how much its dust dims and reddens the stars behind it, tens of thousands of them, and the map shows about 160 small, dense cores strung along the cloud. Most of them are not yet heavy enough to collapse, held up by the warmth and pressure of their own gas, which makes the Pipe a rare view of the moment just before a nursery switches on.

IC1396.beat: Nursery: one generation sparks the next
IC1396.question: How much of the cloud at IC 1396's edge is actually turning into stars?
IC1396.why: Every star begins in a cloud, and in IC 1396 a young cluster and the cold gas around it share one field, the raw material and the first results side by side.
IC1396.look: Start at the Garnet Star and move about a degree and a half south-south-west to the scatter of stars around HD 206267. That bright central star is the group of hot stars doing the work; the glowing gas they press on is faint at best in binoculars.
IC1396.answer: So far only about five percent of the mass of the dark globule called the Elephant's Trunk has turned into protostars. Much of the rest will be boiled away by the hot stars' light before it can collapse, which is why clouds make stars so wastefully, and why their families soon find themselves standing in the open.
IC1396.story: The hot stars at the center are pushing a front of compressed gas into the cloud around them, and new stars form where that front arrives. Inside the Elephant's Trunk the young stars grow younger the deeper they lie in the globule, the pattern expected if the squeeze is moving inward and setting off collapse as it goes.

M17.beat: Nursery: the lights just switched on
M17.question: How long ago did the stars lighting the Omega Nebula switch on?
M17.why: This story starts where gas turns into stars, and the Omega Nebula is a nursery so young that its newborns are still half hidden in the dust they formed from.
M17.answer: They switched on less than a million years ago, a blink in the life of a star like the Sun. The heavy newborns are still wrapped in their cloud, but their light is already eating it away, and within a few million years the gas will be gone and only a bare cluster will remain.
M17.story: Some of the Omega's newest heavyweights are still so deeply buried that only infrared and radio light gets out, and around each one the gas is lit in a small, dense bubble a fraction of a light-year across. That is the very first stage of a heavy star clearing its surroundings, and in time those bubbles will open into the big glowing cavity you see.

M42.question: How does a cold cloud of gas turn itself into stars?
M42.why: Every star's life begins inside a cloud like this, and the Orion Nebula is the nearest place where heavy stars are being made, close enough for binoculars to show their handiwork.
M42.look: Look into the bright core of the glow, where a knot of newborn stars merges into a single point at this power. Everything gray around it is gas their light has reached, and the dark notch biting into one side is dust lying in front of it.
M42.answer: Gravity does it. Where the cloud is densest, a clump of gas pulls itself inward and heats up as it falls, until its center is hot enough to fuse hydrogen and a star switches on. The newborns at the core are already pushing back on the cloud with their light, and that push is how a nursery starts turning into a cluster.
M42.story: Infrared cameras, which see through the dust, find more than a thousand young stars in the nebula's heart, many still wrapped in flat disks of gas and dust. Hubble photographed dozens of those disks as dark silhouettes against the glow, and in them you can see the Sun's own beginning: a young star, a disk around it, and the raw material of planets.

M78.question: What kind of stars is the dark cloud behind M78 making?
M78.why: This story begins with the cloud, and M78 is a small lamp held up against one of Orion's great dark clouds, showing a little of what goes on inside.
M78.answer: It is making mostly small ones. ESO counts about 45 young, low-mass stars in this cloud, still shrinking and settling toward steady adult life, around the two hotter stars whose light you see scattered by dust. Stars like the Sun are born this way, in modest batches deep inside clouds that will one day disperse and let the family go.
M78.story: Stars this young give themselves away twice: in infrared light, because the dust still wrapped around them is warmed and glows, and in X-rays, because newborn stars flare far more violently than grown ones. Those two signatures let astronomers count a family that visible light cannot reach, and they show the cloud behind M78 still at work.

M8.question: Which came first here, the glowing cloud or the stars sitting in it?
M8.why: A star's story begins in cold gas, and the Lagoon is a nursery caught at work, near enough that you can see both the raw material and some of what it has already made.
M8.look: Hold the Lagoon in the middle of the field and compare its two halves: on one side of the dark lane a ragged scatter of stars sits on the glow, on the other a brighter patch of gas with few stars at all.
M8.answer: The cloud came first, and the stars are its children: the ragged scatter beside the lane formed from this gas only about two million years ago. The bright patch across from it is lit by a young star still buried in the gas, and over the next few million years the newborns' light will clear the cloud away and leave their family standing on its own.
M8.story: The ages here come from the smallest members, because a star of the Sun's weight takes tens of millions of years to shrink to its steady adult size. Finding the Lagoon's faint stars still large and contracting dates the whole family. That clock and the hot stars still lighting the gas tell the same story, of a family only just made.

NGC3372.question: How can a star nursery already hold a star close to its death?
NGC3372.why: The whole life of a star starts in clouds like this one, and the Carina Nebula is the grandest nursery binoculars can show, with a twist that makes it the perfect place to begin.
NGC3372.look: Sweep the bright, ragged haze and find the small orange point beside its dark notch of dust. That point is Eta Carinae, a pair of enormously heavy stars born in this very cloud.
NGC3372.answer: Heavy stars live fast. The clusters buried in this cloud are only a few million years old, yet for Eta Carinae that is most of a lifetime: in the 1840s it threw off more than ten Suns' worth of gas and survived. The lighter stars born beside it are only starting out, and they will drift away as a family long after it is gone.
NGC3372.story: Its buried clusters hold dozens of the hottest kind of star, and their combined light and winds are carving the cloud's edges into ridges and pillars. In infrared images the tips of those pillars hide stars so young that they are still firing jets of gas, so the cloud is making stars and being destroyed by them at the same time.

NGC7000.question: How many stars has the North America Nebula already made?
NGC7000.why: A star's life starts in a cloud like this, and the North America Nebula is a whole continent of glowing hydrogen whose newborns are almost all hidden from your eyes.
NGC7000.answer: Spectra have picked out about 580 young stars in and around the cloud, most of them too faint or too veiled by dust for binoculars, and the cloud is still making more. Once the hottest of them have cleared the gas away, the survivors will stand in the open as a cluster.
NGC7000.story: The North America Nebula and the Pelican beside it are one cloud, cut in two by a lane of dust lying in front of them. Along the Pelican's bright rim, infrared telescopes see the cloud being pressed and worn away by starlight, with newborn stars still blowing jets out of the ridges where the squeeze is strongest.

AST-OrionBelt.question: What will become of the three bright Belt stars themselves?
AST-OrionBelt.why: The Belt stars are newborn siblings from the same cloud complex as the Orion Nebula, already loosely spread across the sky.
AST-OrionBelt.look: Put the middle Belt star in the center and follow the S-shaped chain of fainter stars winding between the three. Many of them belong to the same young group, born only a few million years ago.
AST-OrionBelt.answer: Being the heaviest, they will be the first to go: two of them are already supergiants, and all three will most likely end in supernovae, enriching the very clouds where Orion is still making stars. The many small siblings around them will be left to grow old slowly, scattered so widely that no one will see them as a family.
AST-OrionBelt.story: Orion has been making stars in waves for about ten million years: the Belt belongs to one of the older waves, the Sword below it to younger ones, and the Orion Nebula to the youngest of all. Astronomers read that order from the heaviest members, whose short lives make them precise clocks, since a star of twenty or thirty Suns cannot live much beyond five to ten million years.

Cr69.question: Why might one of these newborn stars have died before its siblings grew up?
Cr69.why: The λ Orionis Cluster is a family of newborns that has already cleared a vast space around itself, perhaps with the help of a sibling's death.
Cr69.look: Aim at the faint star of Orion's head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn it into a neat triangle with a dozen fainter stars around it, and notice what is missing: there is no glow at all.
Cr69.answer: If one did, it was the heaviest, because a heavier star squeezes its core harder, the core runs hotter, and the fuel burns disproportionately fast. The biggest member of a family can live only a few million years while its small siblings get billions, which may be how a supernova came to blow this ring clear while its siblings were still young. Every cluster in this story ages from the top down in just this way.
Cr69.story: Around the cluster lies a ring of gas and dust nearly two hundred light-years across, plain in infrared and radio maps, with the family close to its center. The ring's size and the speed at which it is expanding fit a blast about a million years ago, and that is the main reason astronomers suspect one sibling has already finished its life.

IC2395.beat: Newborn cluster, just out of its cloud
IC2395.question: Why does IC 2395 still sparkle with hot blue-white stars?
IC2395.why: IC 2395 is a family that has only just shed its birth cloud.
IC2395.answer: IC 2395 is only about seven million years old, too young for even its heaviest members to have burned out. As they go, one weight class at a time, the cluster will dim and redden like an older family.
IC2395.story: Young stars are born with disks of dust and gas around them, and those disks fade within a few million years as planets form and the stars' light blows the rest away. Infrared surveys find few of IC 2395's stars still carrying them, a second clock that agrees the family has only just stepped into the open.

IC2944.question: How old are the stars eating away the Running Chicken's cloud?
IC2944.why: The young cluster in the Running Chicken's glow is a family of newborns in the middle of destroying its cradle.
IC2944.answer: By Gaia's measurements of its members they are about four million years old. In another few million years the cloud will be gone, and the group will stand in clear space as a young family, the stage that follows every nursery.
IC2944.story: A glowing cloud around a cluster is itself a clock, because hot stars destroy their birth gas within roughly ten million years of switching on: wherever bright gas still surrounds a family, the family must be young. Here the gas is already patchy and broken into knots, the look of a cradle in its last stage.

M16.question: What will be left of the Eagle Nebula once its pillars are gone?
M16.why: In the Eagle Nebula you can watch a newborn family breaking out.
M16.look: Look for the tight scatter of a dozen stars and the dim haze around them, brighter on one side. The stars are the newborns, a few million years old; the haze is the remains of their cloud, which they are slowly destroying.
M16.answer: What will be left is the stars themselves, about 3,500 Suns' worth of them, standing in clear space. The last ones to form, inside the pillars at the very end, will be the family's youngest members, and once the gas has evaporated the whole group begins its long life as a cluster in the open.
M16.story: The cluster's age comes from both ends of the family at once. Its heavy stars are still burning hydrogen in their cores, while its light ones are still shrinking toward adulthood, and only an age under ten million years fits both. That makes the Eagle a cradle caught in the middle of its destruction, neither a fresh cloud nor an empty one.

M21.beat: Newborn cluster that has left its cloud
M21.question: How many stars did M21 take with it out of its cloud?
M21.why: M21, a short sweep from the Lagoon, shows what that cloud's family will look like a few million years on.
M21.answer: Gaia counts about 210 members, together weighing about 900 Suns, most of them far too faint for binoculars. From here on the family can only lose stars: the heaviest will burn out first, and the lightest will slowly slip away into the Galaxy, which is the story of every cluster.
M21.story: M21's age is read the same way from both ends: its heaviest stars are still burning hydrogen, which caps the age, while its lightest are still contracting toward adulthood, which says how recently they formed. Together they place it just ahead of the Lagoon's newborns, the same star-forming region's work caught one stage later.

Mel15.question: How heavy a family is being born inside the Heart Nebula?
Mel15.why: The cluster at the center of the Heart Nebula is a newborn family still wrapped in the gas it came from.
Mel15.answer: The family weighs about 2,700 Suns, its members ranging from eight known O stars, the hottest and heaviest kind, down to a multitude of small ones. The O stars will be gone within a few million years, but the lighter majority will grow up together as a family in the open once the cloud has been blown away.
Mel15.story: The family's light has hollowed a cavity in its cloud, and around the walls the gas is pressed into dense knots and pillars where a younger generation is forming. Infrared surveys find many of those younger stars along the walls rather than at the center, the pattern expected when one family sets off the next.

NGC1981.question: Is NGC 1981 related to the newborn stars in the Orion Nebula?
NGC1981.why: NGC 1981 stands at the top of Orion's Sword, a degree away from the cloud that is still making stars.
NGC1981.look: Start at the Orion Nebula and move about a degree north. Compare the two views: a glowing cloud with its stars inside, then a sparse group of a dozen stars on a clean, dark background.
NGC1981.answer: They are relatives from the same great cloud, born in different waves. Orion has been making stars for millions of years, and NGC 1981 belongs to an earlier wave than the Nebula's newborns, which is why it has already lost its gas and they have not. A cluster's surroundings are a clock, and this one says the family has only just left home.
NGC1981.story: Gaia's measurements show that Orion's young stars are not one family but several groups stacked along the line of sight, each with its own distance, motion and age. NGC 1981 is one of the older groups, and its stars have had time to drift a little away from the cloud they came from, which is why they now stand on clear sky.

NGC2244.beat: Newborn cluster blowing its cloud away
NGC2244.question: What happens to a cloud once its newborn stars switch on?
NGC2244.why: The Rosette Cluster shows a family of newborns pushing its own cloud aside.
NGC2244.look: Go about a third of the way from Betelgeuse to Procyon and drop slightly south into Monoceros, to a small rectangle of stars. Its white stars are the newborns, the one yellow-orange star among them is not a sibling, and on a very dark night the faint ring of haze around the group is what is left of their cloud.
NGC2244.answer: The newborns push it away. Their winds and light have already hollowed out the middle of their cloud, leaving the Rosette Nebula as a glowing ring around an empty heart. In a few million years the ring will thin and fade too, leaving the family under clear skies.
NGC2244.story: The hollow at the Rosette's center is no accident, for the cluster's hottest stars blow winds at a couple of thousand kilometers per second. Those winds, with the push of their light, have driven the gas outward into a thick shell. X-ray telescopes find the cavity filled with gas at millions of degrees, the spent wind itself, still pressing on the ring.

NGC2264.beat: Newborn cluster, still in its cloud
NGC2264.question: Is the Christmas Tree Cluster finished being born?
NGC2264.why: The Christmas Tree Cluster is a family caught in the middle of hatching, its stars already shining while their birth cloud is still around them.
NGC2264.look: Find S Monocerotis, the bright trunk star, and the narrow triangle of fainter stars hanging from it. The gas around them does not show in binoculars, but every star in that triangle formed from it within the last few million years.
NGC2264.answer: It is not quite finished: at the tree's tip the dark Cone Nebula is still collapsing into new stars, even as the older siblings below wear it away. Within a few million years their light will have cleared the last of the gas, and the family will stand in the open.
NGC2264.story: The Christmas Tree has not been born all at once: the members around S Monocerotis, near the base, are older, while the youngest, still hidden in dust, crowd toward the Cone at the tip, where the gas is densest. Ages measured star by star across the cluster follow that gradient, so the tree has been lighting up from one end to the other.

NGC2362.beat: Newborn cluster, one star already aging
NGC2362.question: Why does τ Canis Majoris age faster than all its siblings?
NGC2362.why: The τ Canis Majoris Cluster is a newborn family in which the heaviest sibling has already raced ahead into old age.
NGC2362.look: Find τ Canis Majoris and its tight knot of faint stars. The bright point at the center is the cluster's heaviest member, and the faint stars around it are siblings of the same age that have barely started their lives.
NGC2362.answer: Its weight sets its pace. Its core is crushed harder and burns hotter than a small star's, so it spent its core hydrogen in a few million years and has begun to swell, while the faint stars around it will need billions of years to do the same.
NGC2362.story: The bright point is itself a small crowd: τ Canis Majoris is a multiple star whose brightest member is a hot bright giant, together with a pair of heavy stars that eclipse each other every 1.3 days. So the family's heaviest siblings are packed into one point of light, and every one of them will be gone long before the cluster's small members have settled down.

NGC3293.beat: A young family in the open, an earlier wave
NGC3293.question: What will the Carina Nebula's clusters look like once their gas is gone?
NGC3293.why: The Gem Cluster is an earlier wave of the Carina Nebula's births, a family already standing in the open beside the cloud that is still making its younger siblings.
NGC3293.look: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula move about two degrees north-west to the compact, bright clump of the Gem Cluster. Glowing gas, then a clean knot of stars: the before and after of a cluster's birth.
NGC3293.answer: They will look much like the Gem Cluster does now: a compact knot of about 1,400 Suns' worth of stars, some 320 of them counted by Gaia, standing in clear space at an age of about fifteen million years. The clusters still buried in the nebula are on the same road, ready to begin their long lives as families in the open.
NGC3293.story: Eleven of the Gem Cluster's heavy blue stars quiver every few hours, β Cephei stars whose surfaces rise and fall like a struck bell, one of the richest such choirs known. The notes are set deep inside, where core hydrogen is slowly turning to helium, so they let astronomers listen to how far those heavyweights have come and check the family's age from within.

NGC6231.question: What will NGC 6231 look like when its blazing stars are gone?
NGC6231.why: NGC 6231 is a newborn cluster still full of the heaviest stars a cloud can make.
NGC6231.answer: It will look much fainter and redder. Within a few tens of millions of years all its blue-white heavyweights will have exploded or collapsed, leaving cooler blue-white stars and a few red supergiants as its brightest, the look of an older family. Mass sets the order of departure, heaviest first.
NGC6231.story: Many of NGC 6231's heavy stars come in close pairs, and following the pairs around their orbits weighs them directly: most come out between about ten and forty Suns. Weights like those are how astronomers know this family will soon start losing its brightest members, one supernova at a time.

NGC6530.beat: Newborn cluster, still in its cloud
NGC6530.question: How big a family can one cloud make at once?
NGC6530.why: NGC 6530 is a newborn family so fresh that it still sits on the glowing gas of the Lagoon.
NGC6530.answer: This cloud has produced about 680 known siblings so far, weighing over 2,000 Suns together, all made from the gas still glowing around them, and Gaia's census misses the faintest. Because a cloud makes its whole family at once, every member shares one birthday, and that is what lets astronomers read a star's age from the company it keeps.
NGC6530.story: A newborn cluster mixes stars at very different points of the same beginning: its heavy members already burn hydrogen as adults, while the light ones are still contracting and still wrapped in disks. Spectra of the faint members show lithium, a fragile element young stars have not yet had time to destroy, and that is how astronomers prove they are true newborns rather than older stars lying in front.

NGC6823.beat: Newborn cluster, still in its cloud
NGC6823.question: How many stars has NGC 6823 already made from its cloud?
NGC6823.why: NGC 6823 is a cluster only a few million years old that still sits in its birth cloud.
NGC6823.answer: Gaia counts about 175 members, together about 1,600 Suns' worth, and binoculars catch only the brightest. Once their light has eroded the last of the cloud, those stars will be a family in the open, the next stage in a star's life.
NGC6823.story: In a cluster this young the stars still show their birth order: the heaviest are already burning hydrogen in their cores, while most of the lighter ones are still shrinking and warming toward that point. Astronomers fit both groups to models of how stars of each mass settle down, and the youngest members give the age of the whole family.

NGC6871.beat: Newborn cluster that lost a member
NGC6871.question: What did NGC 6871's lost sibling leave behind?
NGC6871.why: NGC 6871 is a compact knot of hot young stars in the Cygnus Milky Way, and one of its siblings is already missing.
NGC6871.look: From η Cygni move about two degrees east-north-east to a compact scatter of fairly bright white stars. These are hot, heavy young siblings; the one that is missing became something you cannot see at all.
NGC6871.answer: It very likely left a black hole of about twenty Suns, Cygnus X-1, which moves with this group and probably came from a star born with more than forty. The heaviest siblings still shining here will follow it before long, while the lighter ones will grow up into the long-lived family that every cluster eventually becomes.
NGC6871.story: To tie a black hole to a cluster, astronomers measure its motion through space, from the slow drift of its companion star across the sky and the shift of its spectral lines. They compare that with the motion of the cluster's stars, and if the two match, they very likely set out together. Cygnus X-1 passes that test, which turns a lone black hole into a family member with a known age.

NGC7160.question: What comes next for a family that has just finished being born?
NGC7160.why: NGC 7160 shows what the young stars of nearby IC 1396 will look like once their cloud is gone.
NGC7160.answer: A long life in the open comes next. With its gas and most of its planet-making disks gone after about ten million years, its roughly 150 known members will now age together, the heaviest first, while the Galaxy's tides slowly pull the group apart.
NGC7160.story: NGC 7160 is the oldest step in a sequence that runs across Cepheus: the cluster inside IC 1396 is younger, and newborns are still forming at that cloud's edge. Star birth seems to have swept through the region in waves, each generation's light and winds pressing on the gas that makes the next.

AST-Hyades.question: Which of the Hyades have already grown old?
AST-Hyades.why: The Hyades are near enough that you can pick out, star by star, the members that have already grown old.
AST-Hyades.look: Sweep along each arm of the V and stop on every orange-tinted star among the white ones. Leave out Aldebaran, the brightest orange point: it is not part of the family.
AST-Hyades.answer: Four of them have grown old: γ, δ¹, ε and θ¹ Tauri, the orange giants of the V. They were the heaviest stars the family had left, so they ran out of core hydrogen first and swelled. All four are at the same stage of old age, which is exactly what siblings of equal weight and equal age should show.
AST-Hyades.story: Because the Hyades are so close, astronomers can plot hundreds of members by color and true brightness and see exactly where the family's stars peel away from the band of steady adults. That turn-off, at stars a little over twice the Sun's mass, is the clock, and the heavier siblings that once stood above it have left a trace: several white dwarfs, their cooling cores, still travel with the cluster.

IC2391.beat: A young family in the open
IC2391.question: What will the Omicron Velorum Cluster look like in a few hundred million years?
IC2391.why: The Omicron Velorum Cluster is a young, nearby family early in its long life in the open.
IC2391.answer: It will look fainter, warmer and thinner. Its blue-white heavyweights will have swollen into giants and died, its brightest survivors will be white stars, and the Galaxy's tides will have pulled away many of its members, the path every family follows.
IC2391.story: At this age the cluster is a laboratory for how stars settle down: its Sun-like members still spin fast and flare often, while its heavy members are steady blue-white adults. Comparing families of known age like this one with older ones is how astronomers learned that a star's spin and its outbursts fade as it grows up.

IC2602.beat: A young family in the open
IC2602.question: How long until the Southern Pleiades show their first orange giant?
IC2602.why: The Southern Pleiades are a young family early in their life in the open, still sparkling blue-white.
IC2602.answer: It will take a long while by human standards and a short one by a star's. The blue-white heavyweights at its top will go first, swelling into giants as their core hydrogen runs out. Only after that will this family start to look like an older cluster, with warm-tinted giants among white stars.
IC2602.story: Gaia's census of stars moving with the Southern Pleiades finds far more siblings than the compact group you see: a wide halo of members spread over many degrees, stars already working their way out of the family. A cluster starts to dissolve almost as soon as it leaves its cloud, and this halo is that loss caught early.

IC4651.question: Who is left in a star family after 1.7 billion years?
IC4651.why: IC 4651 is a family that has stayed together for nearly two billion years, a rare survivor.
IC4651.answer: What is left is stars much like the Sun and a few aging giants. Everything much heavier has already swollen and died, so the giants at its top are the latest members to reach old age.
IC4651.story: Siblings in a family like this start out with nearly the same chemistry, down to the last trace element, because they formed from one well-mixed cloud. That shared fingerprint outlasts the family itself, and astronomers hope to use it to find the Sun's own lost siblings among the stars around us.

IC4665.beat: A young family in the open
IC4665.question: Which of IC 4665's stars will be the first to grow old?
IC4665.why: IC 4665 is a young family, a few tens of millions of years into its life in the open.
IC4665.answer: The brightest blue-white ones will go first, because they are the heaviest. When their core hydrogen runs out each will swell into a giant and then die, starting a slow change that will leave the family warmer in color, fainter and much sparser.
IC4665.story: IC 4665 is young enough that its smallest red dwarfs are still shrinking toward their adult size, while its heaviest members are already steady blue-white stars. It sits in the long stretch of a family's life when nothing changes at the top, so the next visible change, a first giant, is still many millions of years away.

IC4756.question: Why do a few of IC 4756's stars look yellow and orange?
IC4756.why: IC 4756 is a family that has held together for nearly a billion years, long enough for its members to start growing old.
IC4756.answer: They were the heaviest survivors, so they ran out of core hydrogen first and swelled. Spread over a much bigger surface, their light now comes from cooler gas, and cooler gas glows yellow or orange. They are the family's elders, the first to reach old age.
IC4756.story: Set beside the Hyades, IC 4756 is a little further along, with brightest steady stars slightly lighter and giants slightly less massive. That is all the difference a couple of hundred million years makes to a family's top. Its stars like the Sun, meanwhile, have barely changed at all.

M11.question: How can a family as rich as the Wild Duck Cluster survive so long?
M11.why: The Wild Duck Cluster is a family with enough stars to keep growing old together, packed into a single tight fan.
M11.answer: It survives by sheer weight. All that mass holds onto its members against the Galaxy's tides far better than a small cluster can. Its heaviest stars have already gone the way of every family's top members, and its brightest survivors are now the ones closest to becoming giants.
M11.story: Over its life the heaviest members have sunk toward the middle while the lighter ones drifted outward, like stones and sand sorting themselves in a shaken sieve, and the outskirts are where a cluster loses stars first. Counting the Wild Duck's members by brightness at different distances from its center shows exactly this sorting, a sign that the family has lived long enough for its own gravity to rearrange it.

M23.beat: A family in its middle years
M23.question: Which of M23's ordinary-looking stars will grow old next?
M23.why: M23 is a family a few hundred million years into its life, with nothing blazing left at its top.
M23.answer: The brightest of them will go next, because they are the heaviest stars still in their steady phase. When their core hydrogen runs out they will swell into giants, and then the next weight class down will follow, so the top of the family keeps sinking toward stars like the Sun.
M23.story: A family at this stage has lost its hot blue stars but has few giants to show for it, because stars of three or four Suns pass through the giant stage quickly and spend most of their lives as steady white stars. So M23 looks plain, a field of similar stars, even though some of its members have already lived and died.

M34.beat: A family in its middle years
M34.question: What is pulling M34's family apart as it grows older?
M34.why: M34 is a family a few hundred million years into its life, still blue-white at the top but thinner than a young cluster.
M34.answer: Passing gas clouds and the steady tug of the Galaxy's tides are pulling it apart. Each encounter loosens a few members, which drift off to orbit the Galaxy on their own, so the family thins while its stars age. Its top stars, still blue-white, are the next to run out of core hydrogen and become giants.
M34.story: M34's white dwarfs, the cores of members that have already died, are a gift to astronomers: knowing the cluster's age, they can work out how heavy each star was at birth. Comparing that with what is left shows that a star born at four or five Suns ends as a core of less than one, so most of its matter went back into space.

M35.beat: A young family beside an old one
M35.question: Why does the little smudge beside M35 look so different from it?
M35.why: M35 shares its field with NGC 2158, a family roughly ten times older, so one view holds two ages of the same story.
M35.look: Center M35 and look at its south-west edge for the much smaller, fainter smudge of NGC 2158. Compare the sparkle of the one with the even haze of the other.
M35.answer: NGC 2158 looks so different because it is far older and far more distant. It has lived more than ten times as long as M35, long enough for every bright blue star to burn out, and it lies several times farther away, so its redder survivors merge into a faint haze. Side by side they show where a young family like M35 is headed.
M35.story: The two families are not related: they lie at very different distances and only line up from where we stand, so they never shared a cloud. That makes the pair a clean comparison, two families of the same kind caught at different chapters of one story.

M36.beat: A young family in the open
M36.question: What will M36 look like once its blue-white stars start to age?
M36.why: M36 is a young family whose top stars have barely begun to age.
M36.answer: It will look much like its neighbor M37, a short sweep away, which is more than twenty times older. As M36's brightest members run out of core hydrogen one after another, they will swell into orange giants, and the whole cluster will dim and turn warmer in color.
M36.story: M36, M38 and M37 form a sequence across Auriga from youngest to oldest, and sweeping through them is like leafing through one family album. The youngest is still blue-white at the top, while the oldest has orange giants among its brightest stars. They are unrelated families, which makes the point stronger, since every cluster ages the same way.

M37.question: Why are M37's few brightest stars orange rather than blue-white?
M37.why: M37 is an old family whose brightest members have already grown into giants.
M37.look: Hold M37 steady and look for the handful of points that stand out from the even glow. Its brightest members today are its orange giants, though at this distance their color is hard to catch.
M37.answer: The stars now at the top are the ones that have just run out of core hydrogen and ballooned. Their energy now leaks out through a vastly larger surface, so each square meter runs cooler, and a cooler surface glows orange. Each of them is a star in old age, swollen far beyond the size it had in the family's youth.
M37.story: In a family this old a handful of swollen giants make up a large share of the light, outshining thousands of steady stars, which is why the cluster's glow as a whole is warmer than a young cluster's. Astronomers measure that combined color in faraway galaxies too, and clusters like M37 are the references for turning it into an age.

M39.beat: A family in its middle years
M39.question: What happens to M39's family as its stars age?
M39.why: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
M39.answer: It ages from the top down. Its brightest white stars are the next in line to spend their core hydrogen and swell into giants. As each one does, the family's light grows a little fainter and warmer, just as it did when its bluest members burned out long ago.
M39.story: Dating a family by its top stars sounds simple, but heavy stars like M39's brightest often spin fast. A spinning star stirs fresh hydrogen down into its core and stays in its steady phase longer, blurring the edge between members still burning and members that are done. That blur is one reason the ages of clusters like this one are so hard to pin down.

M41.beat: A young family with its first giants
M41.question: Why does one star near M41's center glow orange among white siblings?
M41.why: M41 has reached the moment when its heaviest survivors are just becoming the family's first giants.
M41.look: Put Sirius at the top of the field and drop about four degrees south. M41 breaks into dozens of white stars, and near its middle one has a clear orange tint: that is the brightest of its giants.
M41.answer: That star glows orange because lifetimes fall steeply with weight: a star a few times heavier than its sibling carries more fuel but burns it so much faster that it runs out first. After about 150 million years only the heaviest members have got that far, and the brightest of these giants sits near the middle, while the next weight class down will follow one star at a time.
M41.story: At M41's age the stars just leaving their steady phase weigh about four or five Suns, so its orange giants were born a little above that, and they will end quietly as white dwarfs. Any sibling born above about eight Suns lived less than about forty million years, and a family this rich very likely had a few, long since gone as supernovae.

M44.question: Why do the Beehive and the Hyades look so alike?
M44.why: The Beehive has reached the stage at which its first giants are just appearing.
M44.look: Break the Beehive into its white and pale-yellow stars, then hunt for the few warmer, yellow-orange points among them: those are the family's new giants.
M44.answer: They look alike because they are at the same stage of life, and they may even share a birthplace, since their ages and their motions through space are similar. Both have lost every hot blue star and both show a handful of orange giants, the heaviest survivors just beginning to swell, which is how any family looks at six or seven hundred million years.
M44.story: Among the Beehive's white stars is one that looks too young for the family: 40 Cancri, hotter than any other member by more than a thousand degrees. It is a blue straggler, most likely made when siblings collided and merged sometime in the last few hundred million years, and the fresh fuel set its clock back. Families can hide second chances like this, which is why astronomers date them from the crowd rather than from any one star.

M45.beat: A young family in the open
M45.question: Has anyone in the Pleiades family grown old yet?
M45.why: The Pleiades are a family at the bright start of their long life in the open.
M45.look: Look at the color of the brightest members: every one is blue-white, with no orange among them. Keep that picture in mind: in older families the colors change.
M45.answer: None has grown old in a way your eye can see. At about 125 million years every bright Pleiad still shines blue-white and none has swollen into an orange giant, but the family has already lost its heaviest siblings, stars too massive to last this long. Alcyone and the other bright sisters are next in line, and when their core hydrogen runs out they will be the first to swell.
M45.story: There is direct evidence of the Pleiades' lost siblings: a white dwarf, the cooling core of a dead star, travels with the cluster. For it to have finished its life already, it must have been born heavier than about six Suns, a sibling that lived fast and died while the bright sisters you see were still young.

M47.beat: A young family in the open
M47.question: Which shows a later chapter of family life, M47 or its neighbor M46?
M47.why: M47 and M46 share one binocular field while sitting at different points in a family's life.
M47.look: Center M47's coarse scatter of bright blue-white stars, then keep M46, the finer misty patch just over a degree east, in the same field and compare their sparkle.
M47.answer: M46 shows the later chapter. At roughly four times M47's age it has already lost the bright blue members M47 still shows, and its survivors are fainter and more even. A family does not fade all at once but from the top down, losing its brightest stars first.
M47.story: Astronomers date families like these by the heaviest star still burning hydrogen in its core, because each weight class runs out at its own predictable time. In M47 that star is several times the Sun's mass, while in M46 it is lighter, which by the same rule makes M46 the older family, though its faint, even look owes as much to its greater distance as to its age.

M48.beat: A family in its middle years
M48.question: Which of M48's stars are next to become giants?
M48.why: M48 is caught halfway, its blue giants gone and its first yellow giants already among the survivors.
M48.answer: The white stars at its top are next in line. A few of their slightly heavier siblings have already swollen into yellow giants, and as each white star exhausts the hydrogen in its core it will follow, swelling and cooling into a giant of its own.
M48.story: M48's giants are heavy enough to have lit the helium in their cores gently, like a slow fire. In a star under about two Suns the core is so tightly packed when helium ignites that it goes off as a runaway flash, for a moment as powerful as a whole galaxy, though none of it reaches the surface. The Sun will go through one in its own old age.

M50.beat: A young family in the open
M50.question: Will M50 still be a cluster by the time its stars are old?
M50.why: M50 is a family still early in its long life in the open.
M50.answer: Only part of it may still be one. Every pass near a gas cloud and every tug of the Galaxy's tides peels off a few members, and most families dissolve within a few hundred million years. M50's roughly 1,800 Suns' worth of stars gives it a fighting chance, and either way its stars will grow old on schedule, heaviest first.
M50.story: A cluster is held together only by its own gravity, and each member that gains a little speed in close passes with its siblings may climb out and leave. This slow evaporation strips the lightest stars first, since they are the easiest to fling outward, so an aging family grows both sparser and weighted toward its heavier members.

M52.beat: A young family in the open
M52.question: How far into its life is M52's family?
M52.why: M52 is a rich but still young family, early in its life in the open.
M52.answer: M52's family is still near the start. Its heaviest members are already gone, but plenty of hot stars remain, and over the next few hundred million years they will swell and die in order of weight, leaving the family warmer in color and fewer at the top.
M52.story: Astronomers date a family like this by plotting each member's color against its true brightness, and stars of one age fall along one curve. The place where that curve bends away from the band of steady adults marks the heaviest stars running low on core hydrogen. For M52 that bend sits among hot blue-white stars, the signature of a family still young.

M6.beat: A young family, its first giant
M6.question: What will BM Scorpii become as the rest of the Butterfly Cluster grows up?
M6.why: In the Butterfly Cluster one sibling, BM Scorpii, has already raced ahead into old age.
M6.answer: BM Scorpii will be a dead star long before its siblings grow old. Having already swollen into an orange giant, it is in the last stretch of its life, and when it is gone the next-heaviest blue-white sibling will take its place as the family's oldest-looking member.
M6.story: In a family about fifty million years old, the line between stars that have already swollen and those still burning hydrogen falls at roughly seven Suns. BM Scorpii must have been born just above it, and its blue-white siblings below. Stars just under that line will become giants in turn, while everything much lighter will still be steady long after the cluster has dissolved.

M67.beat: An old family the Sun's age
M67.question: Which of M67's stars show the Sun's own future?
M67.why: M67 is a family that has reached roughly the Sun's age, so its stars show where a star like ours is headed.
M67.answer: Its brightest stars show it. The yellow and orange giants at the top of M67 began only a little heavier than the Sun, which is why they have already used up their core hydrogen and swollen while the Sun-like members have not. In a few billion years the Sun will do the same.
M67.story: M67 is one of the few places where you can see the Sun's whole future at once. It holds stars just leaving their steady phase, giants on their first climb, giants burning helium in their cores and, fainter, white dwarfs that are already finished. Lined up by brightness and color, they trace the path the Sun will follow over the next several billion years.

M7.question: Will the yellow giant in Ptolemy's Cluster be the last of its family to grow old?
M7.why: Ptolemy's Cluster is a bright, sprawling family whose top stars have begun to grow old.
M7.look: Look for the yellowish star near the middle of the cluster, among the white ones: a giant, one of the family's oldest-looking members.
M7.answer: It is only the first of many. Each of its white siblings, starting with the heaviest, will run out of core hydrogen in turn and swell the same way, and its smallest members, lighter than the Sun, will outlast them all by billions of years.
M7.story: The yellow giant is a few times heavier than the Sun, and stars of that weight spend only about a tenth of their lives as giants, so a family this size can show only one or two at a time. That is why giants are rare in clusters, and why each one is precious to astronomers measuring how fast stars age.

M93.question: What is left of a star family after 700 million years?
M93.why: M93 has lived long enough to lose its blue stars and gain its first aging giants.
M93.look: Look for the arrowhead of white and yellow stars, evenly bright, with no blue-white heavyweights left to stand out.
M93.answer: What is left is the quieter half of the family. Its heaviest stars burned out long ago, its brightest survivors are white and yellow, and a few have already swollen into giants, the stage every member will reach in its turn, from the heaviest down.
M93.story: At this age the heaviest stars still burning hydrogen weigh a bit over twice the Sun, so every member that has died so far was heavier than that, and nearly all of them will have left white dwarfs rather than exploding. Only siblings born above about eight Suns end violently, and in a family like this those were few and went within its first few tens of millions of years.

Mel20.beat: A young family with an aging star
Mel20.question: Has any member of the Alpha Persei family grown old already?
Mel20.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a young family whose brightest member is not quite what it seems.
Mel20.look: Center Mirfak and compare it with the dozens of blue-white stars around it: Mirfak itself is pale yellow, a different color from its siblings.
Mel20.answer: Mirfak, the bright star at the center, already has: it fits the family's age and motion, yet it has left its steady phase and swollen into a yellow-white supergiant. It was the heaviest of the siblings, so it aged first, while the blue-white crowd around it is still in the prime of life.
Mel20.story: Mirfak weighs about eight Suns by most estimates, which puts it right on the line between the two ways a star can end. A little heavier and its core will collapse in a supernova; a little lighter and it will shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf. How the family's present leader dies is still an open question.

NGC1647.beat: A young family in the open
NGC1647.question: What separates NGC 1647 from the Hyades a few degrees away?
NGC1647.why: NGC 1647 shares a corner of Taurus with the Hyades, two families at very different ages.
NGC1647.answer: Mostly age separates them: NGC 1647 is about five times younger than the Hyades, so its brightest members are still steady blue-white stars, while the Hyades' brightest have swollen into orange giants. Put the two together and you see the same kind of family at two chapters of its life.
NGC1647.story: Ages like these come from the heaviest members still burning hydrogen in their cores, since each weight class runs out at its own predictable time. In NGC 1647 stars of several Suns are still doing so, while in the Hyades nothing above about two and a half Suns is left, a gap of hundreds of millions of years in one corner of Taurus.

NGC1662.beat: A family in its middle years
NGC1662.question: What will the Orion Nebula's stars look like a few hundred million years from now?
NGC1662.why: The Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster, at the western edge of Orion, is a family a few hundred million years down the road that Orion's newborns are only starting on.
NGC1662.answer: They will look much like the Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster does now. By then the Nebula's newborns will have lost their cloud and their hottest members, and the survivors will be a sparse, quiet group whose brightest stars are only now nearing the giant stage.
NGC1662.story: Most families never get this far. By one widely cited estimate, fewer than one in ten of the groups born in clouds survives as a bound cluster to even a hundred million years, because once the gas is gone, so is much of the gravity that held them. NGC 1662 has lasted several times longer, and whether Orion's newborns will hold together as well is far from certain.

NGC2232.beat: A young family in the open
NGC2232.question: Where does NGC 2232 sit between Orion's newborns and the old clusters?
NGC2232.why: NGC 2232 is a young family in Monoceros, a short hop from Orion's nurseries, that has already left its cloud far behind.
NGC2232.answer: NGC 2232 sits just past the hatching. Its birth gas has long been cleared and its stars are still building planets from the debris around them, yet its brightest members are white stars in their prime, none of them swollen into a giant. From here it will age from the top down, like every family.
NGC2232.story: Its age depends on which stars you ask. The lightest members, which destroy their fragile lithium at a known pace, give about 38 million years, close to twice what the same models read from their colors and brightness. The two clocks agree only if these young stars are blotched with dark magnetic spots that make them look younger than they are.

NGC2477.question: What happens to a family as rich as NGC 2477 after 700 million years?
NGC2477.why: NGC 2477 is a heavyweight that has lived long enough for its brightest members to become giants.
NGC2477.answer: It holds together better than most, because its great mass gives it a strong grip on its members. But it ages like any other: its heaviest stars went first, and its brightest survivors, already giants, show the stage every star in it will reach in turn, from the heaviest down.
NGC2477.story: With thousands of members, NGC 2477 is rich enough to show every stage of old age at once. Stars just leaving their steady phase, giants on their first climb and a clump of giants burning helium in their cores are all there, sorted by weight. Its white dwarfs have been counted too, and how far the faintest of them have cooled gives a second age that agrees with the first.

NGC2516.beat: A young family in the open
NGC2516.question: How far along is the Southern Beehive in a family's life?
NGC2516.why: The Southern Beehive is a family about as old as the Pleiades, early in its long life in the open.
NGC2516.answer: The Southern Beehive is still early in its life. Its hottest members are already gone, but its brightest survivors are still blue-white, and none has yet joined the orange giants that mark an older family. From here it will age the way every cluster does, losing its top stars one weight class at a time.
NGC2516.story: Clusters this young still spin fast, because Sun-like stars are born rotating quickly and slow down as their winds carry spin away. Timing the Southern Beehive's stars as dark spots turn into and out of view therefore gives an age of its own. That spin clock agrees with the one read from its brightest members, which is why astronomers trust it for lone stars like the Sun.

NGC3532.beat: A family in its middle years
NGC3532.question: What will the Wishing Well look like a billion years from now?
NGC3532.why: The Wishing Well is a family in its middle years, with its first orange giants already among the survivors.
NGC3532.look: Sweep the Wishing Well's crowd of white stars and look for the few orange-tinted points: those are the family's first giants.
NGC3532.answer: It will look warmer and fainter. Its white stars will have swollen into giants and gone in order of weight, until stars not much heavier than the Sun sit at the top, the way the oldest clusters look today.
NGC3532.story: The Wishing Well is rich in white dwarfs, and because the cluster's age is known, each one tells how heavy its star was at birth. Together they show that a star born at three or four Suns leaves a core of well under one, so most of its weight goes back into space before the end.

NGC4755.beat: A young family, its first red supergiant
NGC4755.question: How long before the Jewel Box's other bright stars turn orange too?
NGC4755.why: In the Jewel Box the heaviest sibling has already raced into old age while the others look on.
NGC4755.look: Center the Jewel Box and find the one orange-red star among its blue-white jewels: a sibling that was born with them and has already swollen into a supergiant.
NGC4755.answer: It will not be long by a star's clock. The brightest blue-white members are heavy enough to be close to the end of their steady phase, and each will swell in turn, heaviest first, while the family's small members carry on for billions of years. The orange star is a preview of their old age.
NGC4755.story: The Jewel Box's top has already begun to turn: several of its brightest blue stars, Kappa Crucis among them, are rated supergiants, swelling while still hot as their core hydrogen runs low. They are on the road the red one took first, and the lighter blue-white siblings below them are lined up behind in order of weight.

NGC6633.question: Is NGC 6633 at the same stage of life as the Hyades?
NGC6633.why: NGC 6633 is a family whose first giants have been studied closely enough to be weighed.
NGC6633.look: Pick out NGC 6633's brightest members against the dense background; under a dark sky a few look slightly warmer in tint than the rest, and those are the family's giants.
NGC6633.answer: It is very nearly at the same stage. At about 550 million years it has lost its blue stars and shows a few yellow-orange giants, and its Sun-like stars have burned their lithium almost exactly as the Hyades' have, despite a slightly different chemistry. Different families, born in different places, reach the same chapter on the same schedule.
NGC6633.story: A second clock runs in NGC 6633's smaller stars, and it is lithium, a fragile element that burns at about two and a half million degrees, far cooler than hydrogen needs. In a star like the Sun, slow churning carries a little of it down to where that heat destroys it. So the longer a family has lived, the less lithium its Sun-like stars keep, and families born far apart can be set side by side on one clock.

NGC752.question: Where are NGC 752's lost stars now?
NGC752.why: NGC 752, well over a billion years old, is a family near the end of its life as a cluster.
NGC752.answer: They are spread through the Milky Way. Over more than a billion years the Galaxy's tides have drawn away so many members that only a sparse remnant is left, while the escapees orbit the Galaxy on their own, indistinguishable from any other star. Its few new giants are the family's elders.
NGC752.story: NGC 752's giants weigh only about twice the Sun, the heaviest stars it has left, and stars of that weight have a quiet future: none of its remaining members will explode. From here on every death in this family will be gentle, a giant shedding its outer layers around a white dwarf.

NGC7789.question: Why does Caroline's Rose look misty rather than sparkling?
NGC7789.why: Caroline's Rose is a massive family that has had well over a billion years to change.
NGC7789.answer: Its brightest stars are no longer much brighter than the rest. With the blue heavyweights long gone, the top of the family is a crowd of giants and near-Sun-like stars of similar brightness, and at about 6,400 light-years they merge into an even glow. Age flattens a family's sparkle.
NGC7789.story: Every member of Caroline's Rose still alive is now too light to end as a supernova, so all its future deaths will be gentle ones: giants puffing off their outer layers to leave white dwarfs. Thousands of such endings lie ahead of it, one after another, as each weight class runs out of fuel.

NGC869.beat: A young family with red supergiants
NGC869.question: How long have the Double Cluster's orange supergiants got left?
NGC869.why: In the Double Cluster the heaviest siblings have already reached the last stretch of their lives, only about 14 million years after birth.
NGC869.answer: They have not long left by a star's clock. They are the heaviest members, swollen into red supergiants because their core hydrogen is gone, and stars that heavy are expected to end as supernovae, astronomically soon. Their blue-white siblings are next in line, heaviest first.
NGC869.story: At this family's age the line between stars still burning hydrogen and stars that have swollen sits at about fifteen Suns, so the orange supergiants were born just above it. Counting how many members sit in that bloated stage, against how many are still steady, is one of the ways astronomers measure how long a heavy star spends as a supergiant.

NGC884.beat: A young family with red supergiants
NGC884.question: What will χ Persei look like after its red supergiants are gone?
NGC884.why: χ Persei, the eastern half of the Double Cluster, already shows its heaviest siblings near the end.
NGC884.answer: It will look a little dimmer and bluer for a while, until the next weight class takes their place. When the orange supergiants have exploded, the heaviest blue-white stars still shining will be the ones to run out of fuel and swell, so the family keeps losing its top and growing fainter.
NGC884.story: The red supergiants of both clusters are variable, brightening and fading by anything from a few tenths of a magnitude to two magnitudes over months and years, the restless breathing of stars too swollen to hold still. That restlessness is how a heavy star's last stage begins: it pushes gas off its surface and starts to lose weight before the end.

Stock2.beat: A family in its middle years
Stock2.question: Why is Stock 2 so hard to see as one family?
Stock2.why: Stock 2 is a big family in Cassiopeia, spread so thinly that the eye barely notices it as one group.
Stock2.answer: Stock 2 has been loosening for a few hundred million years. Its members now spread over so much sky that they barely rise above the Milky Way, and the Galaxy's tides will keep drawing them apart while its stars, heaviest first, grow old.
Stock2.story: A family loosens because the Galaxy pulls on it unevenly: the side nearer the galactic center is tugged a little harder than the far side, and that difference slowly stretches the cluster along its orbit. Gaia has found escaped members around several nearby clusters strung out in faint streams that lead and trail the family, much like the two tails of a comet.

DS-Albireo.beat: Aging giant beside a star in its prime
DS-Albireo.question: Why is Albireo's golden star so much further through life than its blue companion?
DS-Albireo.why: Albireo shows an aging giant and a star still in its prime side by side, probably born together.
DS-Albireo.look: Split Albireo into its gold and blue stars. The gold one is the aging giant; the blue one is still in its steady phase.
DS-Albireo.answer: The golden star began heavier. If the two were born together, about 100 million years ago, the heavier star burned through its core hydrogen first and swelled into a cool golden giant, while the lighter blue star is still in its prime. In time the giant will shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf, and the blue star will take its turn.
DS-Albireo.story: Matching each star's brightness and temperature to models of how stars change with age gives the gold star about five Suns and the blue one three to four. That gap is small enough to look trivial and large enough to set them on different clocks. A star twice the Sun's mass spends its core hydrogen in roughly a billion years; one of five Suns needs barely a tenth of that.

DS-DeltaCep.question: Why does a star start pulsing in its old age?
DS-DeltaCep.why: δ Cephei is a heavy star passing through an unsteady stretch of its old age, its outer layers rising and falling every few days.
DS-DeltaCep.answer: It pulses because aging moved its surface temperature into a narrow band in which a layer of helium inside the star acts like a valve, trapping heat when squeezed and releasing it when it expands. A heavy star crosses that band only briefly as it evolves, so δ Cephei is caught in a fleeting stage of its old age.
DS-DeltaCep.story: δ Cephei's rhythm is itself changing, and that change is the star aging in front of us: a pulsating star that grows pulses more slowly, one that shrinks more quickly. Timings going back to John Goodricke's discovery in 1784 show its period shortening by about a tenth of a second a year, which most models read as the star slowly heating as it crosses that narrow band.

HR168.question: What will Schedar become after its orange-giant years?
HR168.why: Schedar, the orange star of Cassiopeia's W, is a giant among the W's whiter stars.
HR168.answer: Schedar will become a white dwarf once it has lived through its giant years. It will swell further, grow unsteady, cast off its outer layers into space and leave behind its bare, hot core, which will then cool for billions of years.
HR168.story: Schedar has most likely already been through its first swelling and now burns helium in its core, a calm stage; when that helium runs out it will swell again, further than before, before shedding its outer layers. Each of those steps takes less time than the one before, so the rest of Schedar's life is short compared with what it has already lived.

HR1713.question: How will Rigel's life end?
HR1713.why: Rigel is a heavyweight in its late years, far too massive to end quietly.
HR1713.answer: Rigel will most likely end with a bang. It has used up the hydrogen in its core, and stars this luminous usually end as core-collapse supernovae, perhaps after first swelling into a red supergiant like Betelgeuse across Orion. When nothing is left to burn, its core will fall in on itself in a fraction of a second and the rest of the star will be blasted into space.
HR1713.look: Rigel is the bright blue-white foot of Orion. Swing across the constellation to orange Betelgeuse at the opposite corner: both are heavyweights past their prime, and Betelgeuse shows the cooler, more swollen stage that may lie ahead of Rigel.
HR1713.story: Rigel has left its long hydrogen-burning life behind, though whether it is still swelling toward the red or has already been a red supergiant and shrunk back is debated, since both paths pass through a hot, blue stage. Its faint, irregular flickers, the sign of slow pulsations deep inside, are one of the tests astronomers use to tell the two apart.

HR2004.question: What lies ahead for Saiph, the hot star at Orion's foot?
HR2004.why: Saiph is a heavy blue supergiant that has already left its steady phase, though it still glows blue-white.
HR2004.answer: A short and dramatic old age lies ahead. As its core runs through its remaining fuels, its envelope should swell and cool, perhaps turning it into a red supergiant like Betelgeuse, and a star this heavy is expected to end in a supernova.
HR2004.story: Saiph and Rigel are both heavyweights past their prime, but Saiph's surface is still nearly as hot as it was in its steady years, so it has most likely only begun to swell, while Rigel has cooled further. A heavy star makes that change in well under a million years, so seeing two of them at different points along it, at Orion's two feet, is a lucky snapshot.

HR2286.question: How close to the end is Tejat, the red giant at Castor's foot?
HR2286.why: Tejat is a red giant far enough along that its outer layers no longer hold perfectly still.
HR2286.answer: Tejat is well along. It has ballooned to about 110 times the Sun's width, and giants this swollen go on to swell further and pulse more strongly, until their outer layers drift off into space.
HR2286.story: Tejat is about twice the Sun's weight, and stars like it spend roughly a tenth of their lives as giants of one kind or another, so it has been aging quickly by a star's standards. When it finishes it will leave a white dwarf of perhaps six-tenths of a Sun, having given back to space well over half of the matter it was born with.
HR2286.look: Find Gemini's western foot: Tejat is the orange-red star there, with the cluster M35 about 3½° to its west-north-west, past Propus (η Geminorum) and a little north. Its deep orange-red is the color of a surface that has swollen to many times its old size and cooled.

HR2326.beat: Aging giant: a heavy star burning helium
HR2326.question: What is Canopus burning now that its core hydrogen is gone?
HR2326.why: Canopus is a heavy star, about 25 million years old and already well past its steady phase.
HR2326.answer: Canopus is most likely burning helium. Models of a star of nine or ten Suns place it in a stage where helium is burning into carbon in its core, a later fuel that lasts far less time than hydrogen did. When that runs out it will swell again, and for a star of its weight the end may come as a heavy white dwarf or a supernova; it sits close to the line between the two.
HR2326.story: Astronomers place Canopus by asking which stage lasts long enough to be caught. A heavy star races through the swelling that follows its core hydrogen in well under a million years, but then burns helium for a couple of million. A star found at Canopus's size and temperature is therefore far more likely to be in that longer stage.

HR2773.question: Where is Pi Puppis in its life story?
HR2773.why: Pi Puppis is a heavy star in its late years, a cool orange supergiant in the Stern of the old ship Argo.
HR2773.answer: Pi Puppis is near its end. It has spent its core hydrogen and swollen into a supergiant, and a star that heavy finishes its life soon after, most likely as a supernova, long before the smaller stars scattered around it grow old.
HR2773.story: The sprinkle of fainter stars around Pi Puppis is its own family, and their ages say how long Pi Puppis itself has been alive: only some tens of millions of years. Only a star born many times heavier than the Sun could have reached the supergiant stage in that time, which is how astronomers know which way its life will end.

HR2990.question: Will Pollux's planet survive what comes next?
HR2990.why: Pollux is a giant with a planet, which makes its future personal: it is a rehearsal for the Sun's.
HR2990.answer: Its planet has survived so far: Pollux has swollen to about nine times the Sun's width, still far inside the planet's orbit at about 1.6 times Earth's distance from the Sun. But a giant keeps growing as it ages, and before the end it will swell much larger and shed much of its mass, so whether the planet survives depends on how far the star reaches and how hard it lets go.
HR2990.story: What decides a planet's fate around a swelling star is a tug of war: as the star loses mass its grip weakens and planets drift outward, but tides raised on the bloated star drag close planets inward. Astronomers find fewer close-in planets around giants than around stars in their prime, a hint that the tides often win.

HR3307.beat: Aging giant beside a hot young star
HR3307.question: How can one point of light hold an old giant and a young-looking star?
HR3307.why: Avior blends an aging orange giant and a hot blue star into one point in the False Cross.
HR3307.answer: The two stars started with different weights. The one that became the giant was heavier, so it ran through its core hydrogen first and swelled, while its partner is still in its steady phase. Each pair like this is a snapshot of two chapters of the same story.
HR3307.story: Avior's blue partner is itself a heavy star, about seven Suns of hot blue-white, still calmly burning hydrogen in its core. The two are separated by at least about ninety times Earth's distance from the Sun, too far to have traded gas, so whatever set them on different clocks was settled at birth, not by one star feeding on the other.

HR3634.beat: Aging supergiant: near the dividing line
HR3634.question: Will Suhail end with a bang or quietly?
HR3634.why: Suhail, the orange star in the sails of Vela, is a swollen giant whose weight puts it close to the line between the two ways a star can end.
HR3634.answer: No one can say for certain, because its birth weight has not been measured well. A star born above about eight Suns keeps burning heavier fuels until its core collapses and explodes, while one born lighter sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf. Suhail's light, several thousand Suns' worth, places it close to that line.
HR3634.story: Above the line, each fuel a star burns lasts a fraction of the one before. Hydrogen keeps it going for millions of years, helium for about a tenth as long, carbon for centuries, and the heavier fuels that follow for a year or so, months and finally days. The surface barely notices those last stages, so a supergiant can look calm right up to the end, and nobody can tell from outside how near that is.

HR6241.beat: Aging giant: an ordinary orange giant
HR6241.question: What is ε Scorpii's old age like compared with Antares'?
HR6241.why: ε Scorpii is a modest orange giant just along the Scorpion's body from Antares, a far heavier star at a far later stage.
HR6241.answer: ε Scorpii's old age is slower and gentler. It is an ordinary giant, about twelve times the Sun's width, burning through its later fuels at a calm pace, while Antares is a heavyweight racing toward a supernova. A modest giant like ε ends by shedding its outer layers and leaving a white dwarf, the quiet way most stars end.
HR6241.story: ε Scorpii is a clump giant, a star that has been through its first swelling and now burns helium quietly in its core, a calm stage of about a hundred million years, a small fraction of its prime. Most of the orange giants you see in the sky sit on this same plateau, which is why so many of them look alike.

HR6262.beat: Aging hypergiant: a heavyweight near the end
HR6262.question: How long can a star as heavy as ζ¹ Scorpii last?
HR6262.why: ζ¹ Scorpii is one of the heaviest stars binoculars can show, already in its late years though it was born only a few million years ago.
HR6262.answer: A star like ζ¹ lasts only a few million years in all, and it has spent most of them. Stars this heavy burn fuel at a ferocious rate, and ζ¹ has already left its steady phase to become a hypergiant, unstable and swollen. Its end will be a supernova, or perhaps a collapse straight into a black hole.
