HR6262.story: Stars this heavy blow so much of themselves away in their winds that they can lose a large share of their weight before the end, and how much they lose helps decide what remains. ζ¹'s spectrum shows that wind directly, in lines stretched by gas streaming off its surface.

HR7139.beat: Aging giant: a cool bright giant
HR7139.question: What makes δ² Lyrae so much redder than its blue neighbor?
HR7139.why: δ² Lyrae is a cool giant sitting in one field with a hot blue star, so old age shows plainly as color.
HR7139.answer: Old age has made it redder. δ² has used up its core fuel and ballooned into a giant hundreds of times the Sun's width, and its light now escapes from a surface so cool that it glows orange-red. Giants this swollen are near the end, when they begin to lose their outer layers to space.
HR7139.story: δ² Lyrae is most likely on the last climb of a giant's life, after its core helium is gone, burning hydrogen and helium in two thin shells around a dead core of carbon and oxygen. Its light wobbles slightly and irregularly, as such giants do, because a surface so far from its core is barely held in place.

HR7264.question: What stage of life has Albaldah reached?
HR7264.why: Albaldah, above the Teapot's handle in Sagittarius, is a luminous giant that has only lately left its steady phase.
HR7264.answer: Albaldah has reached the swelling that follows a star's prime. Its surface is still a hot yellow-white rather than orange, so it is early in its old age, on its way to becoming larger and cooler before the end.
HR7264.story: A star that has just left its prime crosses a stretch in which it changes quickly, so astronomers rarely catch one there, and Albaldah's yellow-white surface and size of nearly thirty Suns put it in that brief crossing. Well before the Sun has aged at all, it will have cooled to orange and swollen much further.

HR7525.question: What has old age done to Tarazed, Altair's orange companion on the sky?
HR7525.why: Tarazed is a bright giant whose orange glow stands out right beside white Altair.
HR7525.look: Put Altair and Tarazed in one field: crisp white against warm orange. The orange is old age showing in the color of a swollen surface.
HR7525.answer: It has made it enormous and cool. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, Tarazed swelled into a bright giant many times the Sun's width, and its surface cooled to orange as its light spread over far more area. Its next steps are to swell further and finally shed its outer layers.
HR7525.story: How a star swells has a neat explanation: once the core's hydrogen is gone, the core shrinks and heats, a shell of hydrogen around it ignites, and that shell pours out more energy than the core ever did. The extra heat pushes the outer layers outward until the surface is so large and so cool that it glows orange.

HR7796.question: How far along is Sadr, at the heart of the Northern Cross?
HR7796.why: Sadr is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star grown huge after leaving its steady phase.
HR7796.answer: Sadr is well into its old age. With its core hydrogen spent, Sadr has swollen to about 180 times the Sun's width, and a star that heavy and that swollen is heading for a supernova.
HR7796.story: Models matched to its brightness and temperature give Sadr a birth weight of about a dozen Suns and an age of only about twelve million years, less than a three-hundredth of the Sun's. That is how fast a heavy star reaches old age: by the time a star like the Sun would barely have settled in, Sadr's core hydrogen is spent.

HR911.beat: Aging giant: a red giant, still steady
HR911.question: What will Menkar have to go through to become like Mira?
HR911.why: Menkar is a red giant much like Mira in the same constellation, but one stage earlier.
HR911.answer: Menkar will have to swell further and lose its balance. As it ages its outer layers will grow larger and looser until they begin to rock in and out, and its light will start swinging like Mira's. That restless stage is the beginning of the end, when a giant starts giving its gas back to space.
HR911.story: Whether a giant pulses is set by how large and cool it has grown: up to a certain size its outer layers settle into balance, beyond it they overshoot and rock. Menkar's light holds nearly steady, so it sits on the calm side of that line, while Mira, larger and cooler, has crossed it.

STAR-Capella.beat: Aging giants: two stars, two stages
STAR-Capella.question: What comes next for Capella's two giants?
STAR-Capella.why: Capella holds two old stars in one point of light, born together and caught at slightly different stages.
STAR-Capella.answer: When the heavier one finishes burning the helium in its core, it will swell again, larger and more luminous than now, and its twin will follow the same path a little behind. Stars of about two and a half Suns end quietly: each will cast off its outer layers into space and leave a white dwarf, so Capella will one day be a pair of embers.
STAR-Capella.story: Capella's family has two more members, a pair of faint red dwarfs about ten thousand times Earth's distance from the Sun away, sharing the giants' motion through space. Born at the same moment, they are so light that they will keep burning hydrogen in their cores for far longer than the universe has yet existed, long after both giants have become embers.

STAR-Deneb.beat: Aging supergiant on its way to red
STAR-Deneb.question: What is Deneb turning into?
STAR-Deneb.why: Deneb is a heavyweight whose old age is happening fast.
STAR-Deneb.answer: Deneb is most likely turning into a red supergiant. Its surface already shows nitrogen dredged up from the core, a sign that it has burned through its core hydrogen, and the best models have it swelling toward the red supergiant stage on its way to a supernova. For now it is a white star about 200 times the Sun's width, midway through that crossing.
STAR-Deneb.story: A heavy star burns hydrogen through a cycle that uses carbon as a go-between and turns much of it into nitrogen, so nitrogen showing up at the surface means material from the core has been mixed outward. In Deneb that mixing is strong enough to measure, one of the main clues that the star has finished its core hydrogen rather than still being in its prime.
STAR-Deneb.look: Deneb is the bright white star at the tail of the swan, the top of the Northern Cross. Its white is the color of a heavyweight only partway to red; sweep about 16° north-north-east into Cepheus to the Garnet Star, a deep orange-red supergiant at the stage Deneb is heading for.

HR1607.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
HR1607.question: How long can Hind's Crimson Star keep puffing out its carbon?
HR1607.why: Hind's Crimson Star is a dying giant in one of the last stages of a Sun-like star's life, deep red with its own carbon.
HR1607.answer: It cannot keep it up for long, as stars count time. Each slow pulse helps lift more of its envelope away, and once the envelope is gone the bare core will be left as a white dwarf. The carbon it has given away will drift into the clouds where new stars and planets form.
HR1607.story: The carbon-star stage is brief even by the standards of a star's old age, likely a few hundred thousand years at most, and the reason is a feedback loop. Each flash of helium burning deep inside brings up more carbon, more carbon makes more soot, and soot catches starlight so well that it is pushed outward, dragging gas along. The star is feeding the very wind that will strip it bare.

HR1648.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
HR1648.question: What is W Orionis doing with the carbon it has made?
HR1648.why: W Orionis is a dying giant in Orion that has already started to hand its carbon back.
HR1648.answer: W Orionis is giving it to the Galaxy. Carbon dredged up from its interior forms soot and gas in its cool atmosphere, and its wind carries them away; when the envelope is gone, the bare core will be left as a white dwarf. Orion's nurseries a few fields away show where such material ends up.
HR1648.story: Proof that giants at this stage make their own elements came in 1952, when Paul Merrill found technetium in their spectra. Technetium has no stable form, and the kind these stars make loses half of itself in about two hundred thousand years, so it cannot be left over from their birth cloud. It was made inside, recently, and carried up to the surface, just as W Orionis's carbon was.

HR2405.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
HR2405.question: How will UU Aurigae's life end?
HR2405.why: UU Aurigae is a carbon star, a giant in its last stage that is already blowing its outer layers into space.
HR2405.answer: UU Aurigae will end quietly, by giving itself away. Its slow wind will strip off the rest of its carbon-rich envelope until only the hot core remains, a white dwarf that will cool for billions of years while the gas and dust it shed join the clouds that make new stars.
HR2405.story: Not every giant can become a carbon star; it takes the right weight at birth, roughly one and a half to four Suns. Lighter stars never dredge up enough carbon to outnumber the oxygen that would lock it away, while in heavier ones the base of the envelope runs so hot that it burns new carbon into nitrogen. UU Aurigae's color is a record of the weight it was born with.

HR2748.beat: The end begins: shedding its skin
HR2748.question: What will L² Puppis leave behind when its shedding is done?
HR2748.why: L² Puppis is a dying giant, born about as heavy as the Sun and already down to two-thirds of it, caught letting its outer layers go.
HR2748.answer: It will leave a small, hot core, a white dwarf, which for a few thousand years will light the gas it has cast off as a glowing shell. The dust forming in its wind now will drift into the Galaxy's clouds, and some of it may end up in planets that form long after the star itself has gone dark.
HR2748.story: The ALMA images that weighed L² Puppis also caught a small companion circling about twice as far from it as Earth is from the Sun, a planet or perhaps a brown dwarf. Models suggest the star's swollen envelope will drag it inward until it is swallowed, a preview of what the Sun's old age may do to its nearest planets.

HR3207.beat: On the brink: a star stripped to its core
HR3207.question: What will the stripped star inside Gamma Velorum do next?
HR3207.why: Gamma Velorum holds a heavy star that has already lost its outer layers to its own winds, one step from the finish.
HR3207.answer: It will most likely explode: with its hydrogen gone, the Wolf–Rayet star is burning through the heavier fuels in its exposed core, and when those run out the core should collapse in a supernova. The young stars gathered around Gamma Velorum will be showered with its debris, and the cycle of this story begins again.
HR3207.story: The stripped star must have been born the heavier of the two, because in a pair born together the heavier partner ages first, yet it now weighs about a third as much as its companion. Its winds, perhaps helped by handing gas to its partner, peeled away its hydrogen layers, and its surface now shows carbon made by burning helium, the inside of a star turned out for us to see.

HR3541.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
HR3541.question: What is X Cancri giving back to the Galaxy?
HR3541.why: X Cancri is a dying giant that has dredged carbon from its core to its surface and is now letting it go.
HR3541.answer: X Cancri is giving back carbon, made in its core and carried off as soot and gas in its wind, along with the rest of its outer layers. When the giving is over, a white dwarf will be all that is left of the star, and its carbon will be on its way to future stars and planets.
HR3541.story: Carbon is not the only thing X Cancri makes. In the layer where helium burns, free neutrons soak one at a time into iron nuclei and build them, step by step, into heavier elements such as strontium, barium and lead. This slow process in giants like this one is thought to have made about half of all the elements heavier than iron, and the star's wind carries them out along with its soot.

HR4210.beat: On the brink: a star that nearly blew apart
HR4210.question: How close is Eta Carinae to exploding?
HR4210.why: Eta Carinae, the small orange point inside the Carina Nebula, is a pair of enormously heavy stars near the violent end of their lives.
HR4210.answer: Eta Carinae is close by a star's clock, though no one can name the date. A star this heavy lives only a few million years, and its survival of the Great Eruption shows how near the edge it already is. When it does explode, its debris will tear into the Carina Nebula, the very cloud it was born in, and the cycle of this story will start over there.
HR4210.story: Light from the star's great outburst of the 1840s that set off toward distant dust clouds has been bouncing back to us like an echo, so astronomers can take spectra of an eruption seen by eye long ago. In 2018 those echoes showed gas flung out at more than ten thousand kilometers per second, the mark of a blast rather than a gentle wind, a near-explosion the star somehow survived.

HR6146.beat: The end begins: shedding its skin
HR6146.question: How does a giant like g Herculis give its gas back to space?
HR6146.why: g Herculis is an old giant whose thin outer layers are already leaking away.
HR6146.answer: It gives its gas back a little with every pulse. Each swelling lifts its loose, cool outer layers higher, and some never fall back, so over thousands of years the star strips itself down toward its core. When the core is bare it will be a white dwarf, and the gas it shed will join the clouds between the stars.
HR6146.story: Stretched hundreds of times wider than the Sun, g Herculis holds its surface with a gravity tens of thousands of times feebler than the Sun's, so it takes only a nudge to loft gas. Each pulse sends a shock wave up through its atmosphere that throws gas high enough to cool, and there dust condenses, catches the starlight and is pushed away, pulling the gas along with it.

HR7066.beat: The end begins: an unsteady dying giant
HR7066.question: What is happening to R Scuti in its last stage?
HR7066.why: R Scuti, a degree from the Wild Duck Cluster, is a bloated giant in the last unsettled stage of its life.
HR7066.answer: Its last fuels are nearly spent, and astronomers still debate whether it is in the final giant stage or already leaving it, on its way to becoming the exposed core at the heart of a planetary nebula. Either way the end has begun, and its uneven heaving is the star coming loose.
HR7066.story: R Scuti is one of the few stars whose irregularity has been shown to be chaos in the mathematician's sense. In 1996 an analysis of decades of amateur brightness estimates found that its swings follow a small set of fixed rules that never quite repeat. Two rhythms drive each other in an envelope too loosely held to keep a steady beat.

HR7763.beat: On the brink: a star blowing itself apart
HR7763.question: How will P Cygni's struggle against its own light end?
HR7763.why: P Cygni is a heavyweight so luminous that it is already coming apart at the seams.
HR7763.answer: It will end with its core collapsing, after it has lost much more of itself. Its winds and outbursts strip away mass, like the shell of about a tenth of a Sun it threw off in 1600, and when the core has burned through its last fuel it will fall in on itself, most likely in a supernova.
HR7763.story: Records going back to about 1700 show P Cygni slowly brightening, by about a seventh of a magnitude a century. The usual reading is that its surface is cooling while its total output holds steady, shifting more of its light into colors the eye sees. That would make it one of the very few stars whose aging can be followed through human history, though models explain only part of the change.

HR8262.beat: The end begins: shedding its skin
HR8262.question: What will W Cygni's pulses have done by the time they stop?
HR8262.why: W Cygni is a red giant late in life whose every pulse pushes a little more of it into space.
HR8262.answer: They will have given the star away. Cycle after cycle they lift its outer layers off, until only the hot core is left, a white dwarf that will briefly light the cast-off gas before both fade. The gas itself goes back into the Galaxy, to be used again.
HR8262.story: A giant's pulses change as it nears the end. Small, loose rhythms like W Cygni's are thought by many astronomers to come first, and as the star grows larger and cooler its swings deepen and lengthen toward the deep, regular beat of a Mira. The wind grows with them, so the closer a giant gets to its end, the faster it gives itself away.

HR8383.beat: On the brink: a bloated supergiant
HR8383.question: How close to its end is the giant of VV Cephei?
HR8383.why: VV Cephei holds a red supergiant in the bloated last stage of a heavy star's life, with a hot companion circling it.
HR8383.answer: It is close, as heavy stars count time. It has swollen to hundreds of times the Sun's width and is losing gas from its loosely held surface. Red supergiants like it end when their cores collapse, most likely in a supernova that will shower its companion's neighborhood with debris.
HR8383.story: A red supergiant with a companion this close cannot keep all its gas to itself: its swollen outer layers spill toward the hot star, which is wrapped in a glowing disk of the captured gas. That transfer strips the giant faster than its wind alone would, so a partner can bring the end of a heavy star's life closer.

HR9004.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
HR9004.question: How will TX Piscium's life end?
HR9004.why: TX Piscium is a carbon star, a giant near the end that is filtering its light through its own smoke.
HR9004.answer: TX Piscium will end by blowing itself away. Dust forming close to the star is pushed outward by its light, dragging gas with it, until the whole envelope has gone and only a white dwarf remains. The carbon in that dust will be part of the next generation of stars and planets.
HR9004.story: Herschel's infrared images show the gas TX Piscium has already lost swept into a bow along its path, because the star is plowing through the thin gas between the stars at about 55 kilometers per second. So the handover has already begun: what it sheds does not drift off untouched but piles up against the Galaxy's own gas and starts to mix with it.

HR9045.beat: On the brink: a star throwing off shells
HR9045.question: Where is ρ Cassiopeiae headed after its outbursts?
HR9045.why: ρ Cassiopeiae is a hypergiant in a brief, unstable stage near the very end of a heavy star's life.
HR9045.answer: ρ Cassiopeiae is headed toward collapse. Many astronomers think it has already been a red supergiant and is now heating up again, throwing off shells of gas as it goes. A star this heavy can only end with its core collapsing, in a supernova or perhaps straight into a black hole.
HR9045.story: Yellow hypergiants like ρ Cassiopeiae seem to bounce off an invisible wall. As one heats up, its swollen atmosphere reaches a range of temperatures at which it can no longer hold steady, so it throws off a shell, cools sharply and then starts heating again. ρ Cassiopeiae has done this four times in the last century or so, most recently in 2013, and the gaps between outbursts seem to be shrinking.

M1.question: Will the Crab Nebula's debris end up in new stars?
M1.why: The Crab is the wreck of a heavy star whose explosion was seen from Earth in 1054.
M1.answer: It will, in time. The expanding cloud will thin and merge with the gas between the stars over many thousands of years, carrying elements forged in the star and its explosion. Some of it will one day be gathered into a cloud that makes stars, the beginning of this story all over again.
M1.story: The Crab's glow is powered from inside: the spinning neutron star at its center pours energy into the nebula, which is why it still shines so brightly nearly a thousand years after the blast. Astronomers watch that core slowing down by timing its pulses, and the energy it loses each second matches what the nebula gives off.

M27.question: Is the Dumbbell the end of a star's story or a new beginning?
M27.why: The Dumbbell is what a star like the Sun leaves when it is done, close enough that binoculars show its shape on a dark, moonless night.
M27.answer: The Dumbbell is both. The white dwarf at its center will cool for billions of years and never shine by fusion again. But the gas, carrying elements made inside the star, will spread into the Galaxy's clouds, where future stars and planets will form from it, just as the Sun and Earth formed from material like this.
M27.story: The star at the Dumbbell's center is one of the hottest known, around a hundred thousand degrees, because it is the bare core that once burned helium deep inside the giant. Its ultraviolet light strips electrons from the gas around it, and as the core cools over the next tens of thousands of years the shell will dim until the glow goes out.

NGC6992.question: What will become of the gas in the Veil's blast wave?
NGC6992.why: The Veil is how the heaviest stars end: the expanding wreck of a supernova, thousands of years after the blast.
NGC6992.answer: It will slow, cool and stop glowing over tens of thousands of years, then mix into the clouds between the stars, enriched with elements forged in the star and in its explosion. Shocks like this can even squeeze nearby clouds into collapsing, so the death of one star can start the birth of the next.
NGC6992.story: Spectra show the Veil's gas racing outward at hundreds of kilometers per second, and working back from its size gives an explosion roughly ten to twenty thousand years ago. The arc glows where the shock heats the gas it sweeps up, so most of what you see is gas from between the stars, with a share of the dead star's own debris mixed in.

NGC7293.question: What will happen to the Helix's glowing shell?
NGC7293.why: The Helix is the cast-off shell of a star like the Sun, near enough to look large in binoculars.
NGC7293.answer: It will fade and spread. As the white dwarf at its center cools, it will stop lighting the gas, and the shell will thin into the space between the stars. The elements made inside the star will go with it, into the clouds that build the next generation.
NGC7293.story: The Helix is close enough that its gas breaks up into thousands of comet-shaped knots, each about the size of our solar system, with tails pointing away from the central star. They form where the hot, fast wind of the exposed core runs into the slower gas the giant shed earlier, and in time they too will dissolve and mix with the gas around them.

STAR-Antares.beat: On the brink: a supernova in waiting
STAR-Antares.question: What will Antares leave behind when it explodes?
STAR-Antares.why: Antares, the red heart of the Scorpion, is a heavyweight already near the explosive finish reserved for the heaviest stars.
STAR-Antares.answer: Antares will most likely leave a neutron star, a collapsed core so dense that a Sun's worth of matter fits in a ball the size of a city, inside an expanding cloud of debris like the Veil in Cygnus. That cloud will carry the oxygen, silicon and iron Antares forged in its core out into the Galaxy, ready to be built into new stars.
STAR-Antares.story: Antares will run through its last fuels quickly: after helium come carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon, each burning for a shorter time in a shrinking core, the last in a matter of days. Neutrinos from those final stages pour out so fast that, in the hours before the collapse, detectors on Earth might sense them before any change in its light.

STAR-Betelgeuse.beat: On the brink: a supernova in waiting
STAR-Betelgeuse.question: How soon will Betelgeuse explode, and how can anyone tell?
STAR-Betelgeuse.why: Betelgeuse, the orange shoulder of Orion, is a heavy star close to the violent end that only the heaviest stars meet.
STAR-Betelgeuse.answer: The best models put the explosion about 100,000 years away, a moment in the life of a star, and they rest on how Betelgeuse's light, size and slow pulsations fit a heavy star early in burning the helium in its core. A star this heavy races through its last fuels after that. When its core finally collapses, the rest of Betelgeuse will be blasted into Orion's clouds, the same clouds where new stars are being born tonight.
STAR-Betelgeuse.story: Betelgeuse's famous dimming in 2019 and 2020 gave astronomers a close look at how such a star sheds itself. A great bubble of gas rose from its surface, cooled and condensed into dust that hid part of the star for months. Episodes like that, repeated again and again, are how a red supergiant loses much of its outer layers before its core gives out.

STAR-LaSuperba.beat: The end begins: giving back its carbon
STAR-LaSuperba.question: What will be left of La Superba once its wind has done its work?
STAR-LaSuperba.why: La Superba is a dying giant that has turned red with the carbon it made and is now blowing it into space.
STAR-LaSuperba.answer: La Superba will leave a white dwarf, and around where it stood a shell of carbon-rich dust and gas, already about three light-years across, where its wind has piled up against the gas between the stars. That material will mix into future clouds, the raw stuff of the next stars.
STAR-LaSuperba.story: Even among carbon stars La Superba is odd: roughly one carbon atom in five at its surface is the heavier kind, carbon-13, where the Sun has about one in ninety. How a star like this built up so much is still unexplained, so the carbon it is returning to the Galaxy carries a recipe nobody has fully worked out.

STAR-Mira.beat: The end begins: shedding its skin
STAR-Mira.question: Where does all the gas that Mira sheds end up?
STAR-Mira.why: Mira is a giant at the stage where the end has already begun, pulsing and losing its outer layers to space.
STAR-Mira.look: Check a current brightness estimate first, because near its faintest Mira is out of binocular reach. Near its peak it is an obvious orange-red point in the Whale's neck, well south of Aries.
STAR-Mira.answer: Some falls onto Mira's companion, a white dwarf that feeds on its wind, and the rest streams out into space. In the end Mira will give away its whole envelope, leaving its hot core exposed to light the last of that gas as a planetary nebula, and then to cool as a white dwarf of its own.
STAR-Mira.story: Mira was the first star found to vary, in 1596, and its rhythm is the heartbeat of a giant's last stage: the core is spent, two thin shells burn around it, and the swollen envelope swings in and out every eleven months. Each swing pushes gas out beyond the surface, where it cools into dust that the star's light then drives away.

STAR-MuCep.beat: On the brink: a red supergiant
STAR-MuCep.question: What is the last thing the Garnet Star will do?
STAR-MuCep.why: The Garnet Star is a red supergiant, swollen near the end of a heavy star's life, one of the reddest stars your eye can see.
STAR-MuCep.look: From Alderamin look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. Let the focus go a touch soft and compare its deep orange-red with the white stars around it.
STAR-MuCep.answer: Most likely the Garnet Star will explode. A red supergiant like this is burning through its last fuels in its core, each faster than the one before. When nothing is left that can release energy, the core will collapse and blast the star apart, scattering what it made over a lifetime back into space.
STAR-MuCep.story: The Garnet Star is losing so much gas that it sits inside a shell of its own making, found in infrared light from the warm dust and in radio waves from its molecules. A red supergiant can shed a large share of its mass this way before its core gives out, and how much is gone by then shapes the explosion that follows.

M57.question: What is left once a star like the Sun has run out of fuel?
M57.why: The Ring Nebula is the final page of a modest star's life, the outer layers it let go of still glowing around the core it left behind.
M57.look: Find Lyra's small parallelogram below Vega and aim between its two bottom stars, a little closer to Sheliak. Brace the binoculars: the Ring is a faint star that will not come to a sharp point, best caught under a dark sky.
M57.answer: What is left is a bare, hot core, no bigger than the Earth, and the shell of gas it shed only a few thousand years ago, made to glow by the core's ultraviolet light. Within a few tens of thousands of years the shell will thin into the clouds between the stars, carrying the carbon and nitrogen the star made, and the core will cool in the dark as a white dwarf.
M57.story: The Ring is not really a ring but more like a barrel of glowing gas seen nearly end-on, which is why its middle looks dark. Hubble and Webb images show the white dwarf inside a thin haze, and along the bright rim thousands of small dense knots, clumps of the star's old atmosphere.

HR1325.beat: The end: the ember left behind
HR1325.question: Can binoculars show the core a dead star leaves behind?
HR1325.why: 40 Eridani holds the last stage of a quiet ending, the white dwarf that remains once a star of modest weight has given its outer layers away.
HR1325.look: Find 40 Eridani about 15° west of Rigel, a yellow-orange star in Eridanus. Brace the binoculars and look about 1½ arcminutes to its east-south-east for a very faint point at the limit of braced 10×50s under a dark sky: that is the ember, 40 Eri B. If it will not separate from its bright neighbor, the white dwarf is still there, and so is the story.
HR1325.answer: Under a dark sky, braced 10×50s can just show one: the faint point beside 40 Eridani is a white dwarf, a core of about half the Sun's mass squeezed into a ball the size of the Earth. It stopped making energy long ago and has been cooling on stored heat ever since, the ending that waits for the Sun.
HR1325.story: 40 Eridani B was among the first white dwarfs ever found, seen by William Herschel in 1783, though its nature stayed a puzzle until 1914, when its spectrum showed a white-hot surface on a star far too faint to be large. With no fuel left a white dwarf can only cool, so its temperature today is a clock for how long ago its star died.

NGC3242.question: How long does the glowing shell of a dead star last?
NGC3242.why: The Ghost of Jupiter is the end of the road for a star of modest weight, its cast-off outer layers still lit by the bare core they once wrapped.
NGC3242.answer: The glow lasts only a few tens of thousands of years, because the shell keeps spreading and thinning while the core that lights it cools, so the light goes out long before the white dwarf itself stops shining. The Ghost's inner shell left the star only a few thousand years ago, so this ending is still fresh.
NGC3242.story: A planetary nebula is a brief afterglow. The core left behind is at first hot enough to pour out ultraviolet light that strips electrons from the shed gas, and the gas shines as they are recaptured. As the core cools and the shell spreads, both effects weaken together, which is why these shells are rare in the sky even though they are the fate of most stars.

NGC3132.question: What became of the star that made the Eight-Burst Nebula?
NGC3132.why: The Eight-Burst Nebula is the last page of a star born a few times heavier than the Sun, the outer layers it gave back still glowing around what is left of it.
NGC3132.answer: It became a white dwarf, a faint core hidden beside the 10th-magnitude star at the center, which is only a companion still in its prime; binoculars blend both, and the shell, into one faint point. The star was born at nearly three Suns, lived a few hundred million years, and gave most of that matter back as the shell now glowing around them.
NGC3132.story: Stars born with up to about eight Suns all end this way, which makes planetary nebulae the commonest grave in the Galaxy, though each glows for only a few tens of thousands of years. The shell's shape records the star's last breaths: rings, lobes and bursts like these are thought to be sculpted by companions orbiting close to the dying star.

NGC2440.question: Why does the end of a star like the Sun leave such a hot core?
NGC2440.why: NGC 2440 is a death caught early, the shed layers of a star of modest weight still lit by a core that has only just been laid bare.
NGC2440.answer: The core was the star's furnace, the region where hydrogen and then helium burned, and when the outer layers drift away that buried heat is suddenly exposed at the surface. Its light, mostly ultraviolet, is what makes the shed gas glow, and the glow will fade as the core cools.
NGC2440.story: A star's core gets hotter as it ages, not cooler: each time a fuel runs out the core contracts and heats until the next one ignites, so the very last core of a Sun-like star is the hottest thing it ever made. Stripped of its envelope, that core pours its buried heat out as ultraviolet light, which is why the youngest white dwarfs are among the hottest surfaces in the sky.

HR2693.question: What is Wezen, a creamy-yellow supergiant, on its way to becoming?
HR2693.why: Wezen, the creamy-yellow star in Canis Major's triangle south-east of Sirius, is a heavyweight that has left its prime and is changing fast.
HR2693.look: Wezen is the creamy-yellow star of Canis Major's triangle, south-east of Sirius. Compare it with blue-white Aludra, about 4½° to the south-east, since both are supergiants. Wezen's warmer tint marks a star further along the swelling and cooling that heavy stars go through once their core hydrogen is gone.
HR2693.answer: Wezen is most likely on its way to becoming a red supergiant. It has spent the hydrogen in its core and is swelling and cooling as it goes, already nearly two hundred times the Sun's width. A star that outshines the Sun tens of thousands of times is heavy enough to end its red years by collapsing in a supernova.
HR2693.story: Stars like Wezen are rarely caught, because the crossing from blue-white to red takes only some tens of thousands of years, a blink beside the ten million or so a heavy star spends in its prime. Its tint, cooler than the blue-white stars around it but far hotter than a red supergiant's, is what marks it as most likely mid-crossing, a heavyweight caught between two long stages.

HD58061.beat: On the brink: a giant buried in its own dust
HD58061.question: How much of itself has VY Canis Majoris already thrown away?
HD58061.why: VY Canis Majoris is one of the largest stars known, a red supergiant so swollen that it can no longer hold on to its outer layers.
HD58061.look: From τ Canis Majoris and its little cluster, move about 1¼° south-east to a dull orange point among white stars. It looks faint because it is far away and buried in the gas and dust it has shed.
HD58061.answer: It has thrown away a great deal, at a pace of a hundred Earths' worth of gas or more every year. The arcs and knots that telescopes map around it add up to a large fraction of a Sun lost in the last thousand years or so. A star shedding itself that fast is in the last stretch of its life, and its core will most likely end by collapsing, in a supernova or perhaps straight into a black hole.
HD58061.story: A red supergiant this large barely holds its own surface, because the gravity at its edge is feeble. Pulsations, churning gas and the push of starlight on dust lift material off it in great outbursts rather than a steady breeze. As that gas cools, dust condenses in it and screens the star, so most of its power reaches us as infrared rather than visible light.
